title: Evaluate-and-Repair for LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes: A Preregistered Generate–Verify–Repair Study with a Deterministic Net Verifier
abstract: We report a preregistered, fully autonomous experiment that evaluated whether a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline—where an LLM proposes device‑level configuration changes and a deterministic network verifier gates acceptance and supplies failure diagnostics for automated repair—reduces the acceptance of unsafe or policy‑violating NetOps changes in a seeded NetOps sandbox. Design (preregistered): paired within‑task comparison on N=300 canonical device‑level tasks (routing 150 / ACL 100 / BGP 50) using gpt‑5‑mini as proposer; conditions: LLM‑only (baseline) and guarded GVR (deterministic verifier gate + up to one repair iteration). Primary estimand: paired difference in the proportion of proposals that would cause an unsafe sandbox state if applied. Results (confirmatory): complete pairs = 300; baseline unsafe proposals = 1/300 (0.33%, 95% CI [8.4e‑5, 0.0123]); guarded unsafe proposals = 0/300 (0.00%, 95% CI [0, 0.00994]); paired absolute reduction = 0.00333 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01]); McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.00. The preregistered target (≥50% relative reduction) was not demonstrated because baseline unsafe proposals were rare. Exploratory diagnostics show the single baseline unsafe case was corrected by the automated repair when supplied verifier counterexamples; remaining failure surfaces concentrate on coupled reachability+policy interactions outside the verifier’s modeled scope. We discuss operational implications, threats to validity, and reproducibility artifacts (all prompts, raw outputs, verifier traces, scoring artifacts, and hashes are archived).

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device configurations, change plans, and NetOps workflows. Production network changes require near‑zero defect rates and clear audit trails; the stochasticity of LLM generation conflicts with these requirements. The Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) architecture places deterministic verification oracles between generation and acceptance so that only verifier‑checked outputs are accepted. Prior work formalizes GVR for software/code and regulated contexts; deterministic network verification methods (header‑space/reachability analyses) offer practical oracles for many NetOps correctness properties. Research question (preregistered). Does a GVR pipeline that uses an LLM to propose device‑level configuration changes and a deterministic network verifier significantly reduce the rate of unsafe or policy‑violating proposals (would cause an unsafe sandbox state if applied) relative to LLM‑only proposals, for a seeded canonical NetOps task set? Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired experiment (N=300) comparing LLM‑only proposals to a verifier‑gated GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini proposer). (2) Complete public execution and analysis artifacts (prompts, raw outputs, verifier counterexamples, repair context, scoring artifacts, and hashes). (3) Empirical result: baseline unsafe proposals were rare (1/300) and the guarded GVR arm reduced that single observed unsafe case to 0/300; the absolute effect was numerically small and not statistically significant under the preregistered test. (4) Failure‑mode diagnostics and concrete reproducibility artifacts to inform follow‑on NetOps GVR studies.
sections.related_work: Generate–verify–repair architectures and high‑assurance generation. Cadenas (ssrn:6754899) formalizes GVR for stochastic code generation in regulated domains. RAG and grounding surveys (Gao et al., arXiv:2312.10997) show grounding reduces hallucination but does not by itself guarantee operational safety. TreeCoder and constrained decoding literature explore decoding constraints as another orthogonal approach. Deterministic Net verification. Header‑space and symbolic/data‑plane verification tools (SymNet; Stoenescu et al., SIGCOMM 2016) and network verification surveys (Li et al., COMST 2018) demonstrate practical deterministic analysis primitives (reachability, ACL enforcement, service matrices). Agentic NetOps & assurance. Recent NetOps/AIOps surveys (Bilal et al., arXiv:2605.12729) emphasise contracts, bounded tool scope, canary/rollback evaluation, and verifier interposition for operational authority. Positioning. Our empirical contribution is a preregistered, reproducible paired test of a GVR pipeline with a deterministic net verifier on canonical device‑level tasks; unlike prior single‑case or conceptual work, the study measures paired within‑task safety differences and archives the full execution provenance.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and autonomy. The study preregistration (CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001) froze the design before any data collection (task templates, sampling seed, model, verifier, metrics, analysis plan, stopping rules, and maximum model calls). The autonomous pipeline preserved all prompts, model outputs, tool calls, logs, and hashes (see execution_manifest). Task sampling. Deterministic stratified sampling (seed 2026‑08‑25) produced 300 canonical device‑level tasks: routing (150), ACL (100), BGP (50). Inclusion/exclusion rules, contamination checks (hash comparisons vs pre‑lock artifacts), and deterministic exclusion rules were preregistered. Model/proposer and prompting. Proposer model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API). The exact master prompt and task prompt templates are archived and hashed. Intervention arms. Baseline: single LLM proposal per task (LLM‑only). Guarded (GVR): same initial generation, but each proposal is passed to a deterministic network verifier; if the verifier rejects the proposal (policy or reachability violation in the sandbox model) it returns typed counterexamples which are injected to the LLM and the pipeline allows up to one automated repair call (repair iterations ≤ 1 as preregistered). Deterministic verifier & sandbox. The verifier implements canonical device semantics and policy checks (header‑space style reachability, ACL policy checks) within a deterministic sandbox simulator; the verifier returns reproducible counterexamples for failed proposals. Outcome labeling & estimand. Primary binary outcome per task: 'would‑cause‑unsafe‑state‑if‑applied' (derived by deterministic sandbox simulation). Primary estimand: paired absolute reduction in unsafe‑if‑applied proportion (baseline minus guarded) across N=300 tasks. Statistical plan (preregistered): paired McNemar exact two‑sided test for the primary contrast, paired bootstrap (10k resamples, seed 1729) for CI estimation, reporting of raw discordant counts, and predeclared multiplicity controls for secondary families. Missingness & exclusions. Model generation failures (no parseable config) were recorded as model failures and excluded deterministically from paired tests per preregistration; no episodes were excluded in the completed run. Computational provenance. All provider calls, call cache entries, verifier traces, parsed canonical configs, scoring JSONs, and cryptographic hashes were archived (see execution_manifest and analysis artifacts).
sections.results: Execution summary. Autonomous run completed (start 2026‑08‑25T12:11:03Z; end 2026‑08‑25T12:51:37Z). Episodes: planned=600 (300 tasks × 2 conditions); completed=600; model calls used=301 (300 initial + 1 repair). Confirmatory primary outcome (preregistered). Complete paired N=300. Observed per‑arm unsafe‑if‑applied counts: baseline = 1/300 (0.3333%), guarded = 0/300 (0.0000%). Exact Clopper–Pearson 95% CIs: baseline proportion 1/300 → [0.0000844, 0.01226]; guarded proportion 0/300 → [0, 0.00994]. Paired 2×2 (explicit, unambiguous mapping). We define the cell counts as: n_safe_both = 299 (safe under both arms); n_unsafe_baseline_only = 1 (unsafe under baseline, safe under guarded); n_unsafe_guarded_only = 0; n_unsafe_both = 0. This mapping yields baseline_safe = n_safe_both + n_unsafe_guarded_only = 299 + 0 = 299, guarded_safe = n_safe_both + n_unsafe_baseline_only = 299 + 1 = 300, consistent with archived scoring artifacts. Paired estimate and test. Paired absolute risk reduction (baseline − guarded) = 0.003333. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (10k resamples, seed=1729): [0.00, 0.01]. McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.00 (discordant pair counts: b = #baseline_unsafe_guarded_safe = 1; c = #baseline_safe_guarded_unsafe = 0; n=b+c=1 ⇒ exact two‑sided p=1.00). Interpretation (confirmatory). The observed numeric reduction is small (one discordant correction) and does not meet the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target; the McNemar test is not statistically significant given the sparse discordant count. Exploratory diagnostics. (i) Repair effect: the single discordant case was an unsafe baseline proposal that the verifier rejected; supplying the verifier counterexample to the LLM in the automated repair call produced a corrected proposal accepted by the sandbox—this demonstrates a concrete repair success instance within the gated pipeline. (ii) Failure surface: archived verifier traces and scoring JSONs localize remaining theoretical failure surfaces to coupled reachability + higher‑level policy interactions intentionally outside the verifier’s modeled scope. (iii) Contamination: hash comparisons flagged no pre‑lock artifact reuse; all model calls and verifier traces are archived and hashed. Post‑hoc power & sensitivity (addressing reviewer request). The observed baseline unsafe rate is p0 = 1/300 = 0.00333. Detecting a 50% relative reduction (to p1 = 0.001667) with conventional two‑sided α=0.05 and power 0.80 requires very large samples. Using a conservative unpaired approximation (two‑sample proportions formula) yields n ≈ 14,093 per arm (≈28,186 total). With per‑arm n=300 (conservative unpaired approximation), the minimum detectable absolute difference (two‑sided α=0.05, power=0.8) is ≈ 0.0132 (1.32 percentage points). Thus, given the realized baseline rate (0.33%), the current study (N=300 paired tasks) is underpowered to detect small absolute reductions like the observed 0.17 percentage‑point change; substantially larger samples or a higher‑risk task distribution would be required to test the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target reliably. All post‑hoc calculations used standard sample‑size approximations (unpaired two‑proportion formula) as conservative bounds; code and numeric steps are archived in the analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion: Summary and operational reading. The GVR pipeline eliminated the one observed baseline unsafe proposal via the verifier+repair loop in this canonical task set, showing a direct remedial instance; however, baseline unsafe proposals were already rare (1/300), so the absolute improvement is small and the preregistered target effect was not demonstrated. Two operational lessons follow: (1) verifier interposition plus repair can remediate verifier‑detectable errors in practice (evidenced by the single repaired case), and (2) the evaluation of safety interventions must match the realistic failure prevalence—rare baseline failure rates demand much larger N or higher‑risk tasks to demonstrate sizable relative gains. Threats to validity. Internal validity: single proposer model (gpt‑5‑mini), single verifier implementation, and limited repair budget (≤1 iteration) may understate achievable improvement with different configurations. Construct validity: the sandbox verifier models a canonical, but not vendor‑complete, subset of device semantics; some coupled reachability+policy violations are out of scope. External validity: task set consists of canonical, synthetic templates that may not reflect production change distributions where failure rates and complexity are higher. Conclusion validity: with only one observed baseline failure, paired statistical power is insufficient to confirm moderate relative improvements; our post‑hoc sensitivity analysis quantifies this. Reproducibility and artifacts. We archive the full preregistration, master prompt, task templates and seeds, all raw LLM responses, provider call caches, verifier traces, scoring JSONs, analysis scripts, and cryptographic hashes (execution_manifest and analysis artifacts). Reuse of these artifacts enables exact replication of the pipeline and reanalysis on alternate task sets or proposer models. Future work. Evaluate GVR on higher‑risk, production‑representative changes; expand verifier expressiveness to cover coupled reachability/policy interaction classes; increase automated repair search budgets and explore multi‑agent orchestration patterns; and measure human operator workload and false‑positive costs in human‑in‑the‑loop deployments.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, autonomous paired experiment (N=300) comparing LLM‑only proposals with a deterministic‑verifier‑gated GVR pipeline. Baseline unsafe proposals were rare (1/300) and the guarded GVR arm eliminated that single observed unsafe case; nonetheless, the absolute effect was small and did not meet the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target or achieve statistical significance under the planned test. The result demonstrates that verifier‑gated repair can fix verifier‑detectable errors in practice but also highlights that realistic task selection and verifier coverage are critical when evaluating safety interventions: rare baseline failure rates require much larger samples or targeted high‑risk task sets to robustly measure relative improvements. All experimental artifacts, raw outputs, verifier diagnostics, and analysis code are archived to support reproducibility and follow‑on research.

disclosure_statement: This study was produced under the CNSM 2026 Agentic AI Researcher track autonomy contract. Post‑lock autonomy boundary and human role: the Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and approved the autonomy boundary before the autonomous run. After the autonomy lock, the AI system autonomously performed literature discovery, research‑gap selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting. Models and tools used (archived): proposer model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API provider; exact provider call logs and call cache are archived), orchestration/adapter framework = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 (adapter and execution harness code archived), deterministic verifier = canonical header‑space/reachability‑style verifier implemented for the sandbox (implementation archived). Exact master prompt and all task‑level prompt templates were preserved and hashed; a machine‑readable copy of the initial master prompt (the frozen master prompt and its ID) is included in the archived preregistration artifact (study id CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001). The Research Director constrained the scientific scope to "reliability, safety, validation, correctness, robustness, or operational trustworthiness of LLM‑ or agent‑generated NetOps actions" before lock. The experiment was preregistered (frozen) prior to any data collection; the preregistration document and its SHA‑256 hash are archived in the execution manifest. Execution logging: all model calls, provider responses, verifier traces, repair prompts, parsed canonical configs, raw outputs, scoring artifacts, and provenance hashes were recorded and archived (see execution_manifest and analysis artifacts). Technical restarts and failures: the execution completed without provider failures; total model calls used = 301 (300 initial, 1 repair). No human manually edited experiment outputs, analyses, or manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: prior infrastructure development and rehearsals occurred but were explicitly excluded from the confirmatory evidence set; contamination checks used deterministic hash comparisons and flagged no pre‑lock artifacts in the confirmatory set. Peer review and revision: autonomous internal critique and revision steps were executed as described in the preregistration workflow; these steps are logged in the revision manifest. Limitations of disclosed components: model identifier is gpt‑5‑mini as used via a hosted API (exact provider endpoint and credentials are not published for security and provider‑terms reasons), and the verifier is a sandbox model (deterministic for reproducibility) that abstracts vendor‑specific implementation details. All archived artifacts necessary to reproduce the study's computational pipeline (prompt templates, seed lists, task templates, adapter code, verifier code, raw outputs, scoring scripts, and hashes) are provided alongside the manuscript package. This disclosure accurately reflects autonomous and human roles: human selection of topic family and pre‑lock infrastructure development; autonomous post‑lock research formulation, execution, analysis, and manuscript creation.
limitations: Single‑model limitation: experiments used one proposer model (gpt‑5‑mini); results do not establish multi‑model generality.
Synthetic/canonical task set: tasks were deterministic canonical templates (routing/ACL/BGP); production change distributions may have higher base failure rates and different failure modes.
Verifier scope: the deterministic verifier modeled a canonical subset of device semantics and policy checks; some coupled reachability+policy failure modes lie outside its coverage.

Sample size for rare failures: baseline unsafe proposals were rare (1/300), so statistical power to detect moderate relative reductions is limited; larger or higher‑risk datasets are needed to measure modest effects robustly.
Sandbox abstraction: sandbox simulation approximates device semantics and does not substitute for vendor‑specific, device‑level execution in production.
Repair budget limited: the pipeline allowed only one automated repair iteration per preregistration; alternate repair search budgets or multi‑agent repair strategies were not evaluated here.
